extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/psychology of humor and general readers interested in theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze philosophical and psychological theories of humor (incongruity, superiority, play, comedy vs. tragedy) and their implications for laughter, social functions, and aesthetic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer: Wit as conceptual subsumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit consists in the ability to find for an object a conception under which it can be thought even though it is very different from other objects under that conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Austrian joke and the convict-card anecdote illustrate forming an abstract conception that includes the very case that excludes community. Schopenhauer emphasizes producing a higher-level conception that makes disparate elements fit (Supplement to Book I, Ch. 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when something perceived or thought violates standard mental patterns and normal expectations—i.e., an incongruity between expectation (conception) and perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core is that an element of violation of expectation is present; this can explain puns and wordplay as well as broader comic situations. The text notes that mere perception of incongruity is not always sufficient for amusement (other emotional contexts may block laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution (Schultz/Suls) — puzzle-solving enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: What is enjoyed in many humorous situations is not incongruity itself but the resolution/fitting of the incongruous element into a conceptual schema; after a certain age (seven, per Schultz) people 'get' jokes by reinterpreting the first part so it makes sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unresolvable incongruity is labelled 'nonsense.' Example: Mae West's line 'Marriage is a great institution, but I'm not ready for an institution' depends on shifting meanings and then resolving them; amusement is akin to solving a puzzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Michael Clark's three features of humor (necessary and sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires: (1) a person perceives (thinks, imagines) an object as incongruous; (2) the person enjoys perceiving/thinking/imagining the object; (3) the person enjoys the perceived incongruity at least partly for itself rather than solely for an ulterior reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This refines simple incongruity accounts by adding enjoyment and intrinsic appreciation of incongruity as required conditions (M. Clark in Morreall 1987, 139–155).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beattie's constraint: incongruity insufficient when overridden by stronger emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceiving incongruity does not necessarily produce laughter; stronger emotions such as fear, pity, moral disapproval, indignation, or disgust can attend the same perception and block risible emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to explain why some violations of expectations elicit fear/anger/disgust rather than amusement; historical citation: Beattie (1779).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality Objection to Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (e.g., Kant, Santayana) argue that if humor is enjoyment of violated expectations, it is irrational — how could a delusive expectation gratify? Incongruity itself could not be properly enjoyed by a rational being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an objection theories must address; responses include reframing humor as beneficial play or as a particular kind of cognitive operation distinct from theoretical/practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as play (Play Theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a kind of play — activities engaged in for pleasure that slacken the tension of mental study, provide rest for the soul, exercise abilities in unusual but safe ways, and can have social and cognitive benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and Aquinas view play and humor as legitimate leisure (eutrapelia) when moderate; Aquinas argues playfulness has social benefits and that never being playful is a vice. Modern psychology supports benefits such as stress reduction and social bonding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play signals / Laughter as play signal (ethological account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smiling and laughter are human play signals evolved from ape facial displays (silent bared-teeth social grimace and relaxed open-mouth play face). Laughter (ha ha ha on out-breath) and the play face signal that activity is playful, not real aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Van Hooff and others trace specific facial/vocal transitions from primates to humans; play signals let participants distinguish mock-aggression from real attack and explain why laughter is primarily social.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gricean conversational-maxim violations as a mechanism of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often arises by deliberately violating conversational rules (Grice's maxims): do not say what you believe false; do not assert without evidence; avoid obscurity; avoid ambiguity; be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: breaking Rule 1 (exaggeration, 'pulling someone's leg'); Rule 2 (presenting fantasies as facts); Rule 3 (replying with vague/confusing answers); Rule 4 (prepared jokes that switch interpretations); Rule 5 (turning ordinary complaints into comic rants). Use these to analyze many conversational jokes and puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary / social hypotheses about humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolutionary accounts connect laughter/humor to play and sexual selection (e.g., laughter as social signal, humor influencing desirability). Laughter is overwhelmingly social (we are estimated to be ~30x likelier to laugh with others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: these are hypotheses supported by ethology and evolutionary psychology studies (Greengross, Li et al., Provine). They help explain social prevalence of laughter and male tendency toward playfully aggressive humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's Poetics — comic as non-painful mistake/unseemliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ridiculous is 'a mistake or unseemliness that is not painful or destructive'; both tragic and comic are based on contradiction, but tragic is suffering contradiction while comic is painless contradiction because the comic apprehension sees a way out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to distinguish comic from tragic responses: comic protagonists evoke intellectual/affective disengagement and perception of a non-destructive contradiction; tragic involves despair and loss of hope for a way out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs. Tragedy — social and moral valences
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy embodies anti-heroic, pragmatic responses to life's incongruities (deal-making, trickery, running away), valorizes cleverness and adaptability, uses common speech and broader social cast; tragedy valorizes heroic, emotional engagement and elite figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: comedy models emotional disengagement and thinking through problems, making it allied with philosophical inquiry; comedy's broader protagonists (family, groups) and ordinary language contrast with tragedy's elites and elevated language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's cognitive/rational benefits (play fostering abstraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Playful humor encourages abstract, non-practical modes of thought, allowing one to view failures from a wider perspective (seeing oneself as others do) and thereby fostering rationality rather than undermining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied guidance: in non-imminent-danger contexts, humor enables perspective-taking, reduces immediate personal threat reactions, and promotes mental flexibility and objectivity; but it is inappropriate when immediate practical action is required (e.g., real danger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and psychological benefits of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter reduce stress responses (lower heart rate, blood pressure, epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol), boost immune-system activity, and provide rest for the soul; they thus have health benefits and reduce chronic stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to justify the social/individual value of humor; empirical references include Morreall (1997) and other psychological literature. Note limitations: not a substitute for action in dangerous situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play in development and skill learning (ethological account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Play activities (including humor/play) help young animals and humans learn skills they will use later by exaggerated practice and testing limits of coordination, flexibility, and coping with unexpected situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spinka's observations: young animals' exaggerated movements in play test capacities; analogy applied to human humor: playful violations exercise cognitive and social skills in safe settings, though this doesn't fully explain adult humor's role without additional arguments.
